title: Shares: Australians get a taste for leveraged ETFs
full_text:
Melbourne/Tokyo | Every violent sell-off in South Korea's chip maker giants has become another buying opportunity for Sydney day trader Mark Olsen.
Trading from his home office, Olsen has spent months piling into SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics whenever the shares plunge, often swinging by more than 10 per cent in a single session, as retail investors chase South Korea's artificial intelligence boom with borrowed money.
"You can make a lot more money using leverage," Olsen tells AFR Weekend. "But when everything comes crashing down, that's the problem. We watch guys get wiped out all the time. The volatility is brutal."
And that's what happened this week, when a new breed of leveraged exchange-traded funds tracking the South Korean chip giants tumbled in value, inflicting significant pain on the throngs of punters who opted to risk heavy losses to chase amplified gains.
It's for this reason that Australian ETF providers have warned against the white-knuckle investment strategy as a path to "wealth destruction" for those who don't know what they're doing.
Levered ETFs use debt and financial derivatives like futures contracts and swap agreements to multiply the daily return of an underlying benchmark, typically offering two to three times the daily exposure.
While these products can bring about outsized returns, they also exacerbate volatility as issuers usually need to buy into rallies and sell into declines to keep the funds aligned with their promised leverage ratios.
"Catching a falling knife? It's like having knives thrown at your head and trying to duck," says Olsen, who uses a crypto-trading app called HyperLiquid to place his trades.
Australia has largely avoided the speculative frenzy gripping South Korea's sharemarket, where leveraged bets on the AI chipmakers have become a national phenomenon and sent the Kospi Index up 60 per cent this year, after peaking earlier up more than 100 per cent.
This is partly because the new breed of single stock leveraged ETFs are not permitted in this country. Even so, local investors are still embracing the same high-risk products, with assets in Australia's leveraged exchange-traded funds climbing to $2.3 billion. That's up from $1.6 billion a year ago and about $900 million five years ago.
This mirrors growth in ETFs more generally, which allow investors to buy bundles of shares, or other assets, that track an index or investment theme, and a marked pickup in retail trading, as seen by the rush of Australians trying to snag some shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX when it debuted on Wall Street last month.
There are now 19 levered products available to investors in Australia - more than double what was available in 2020 - that track a mix of Australian, US and global equities, both on the short and long side, along with fixed income. But they have had a decidedly mixed record.
The best-performing leveraged ETF in Australia is Global X's Ultra Long Nasdaq 100 Complex ETF. It's returned almost 70 per cent over the past 12 months, while the biggest laggard is Global X's Ultra Short Nasdaq 100 Complex ETF, which has lost 50 per cent. "Leveraged ETFs are like driving a Formula 1 car - in the hands of a professional and on the right track it can be quite effective, but they're not designed for everyday users," said Global X investment strategist Marc Jocum.
"People are now learning the hard lesson that these are wealth-destroying vehicles over the long term and can cause some destruction if not used appropriately."
In South Korea, it is the single-stock leveraged ETFs that have taken the sharemarket - and the country - by storm, with their massive gains from the AI trade allowing young day traders to splash out on Rolex watches and luxury cars.
The products, which turbocharge bets on the country's tech giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, are the result of a global boom in retail investing coinciding with the market's obsession with AI.
But the massive gains don't come without the equally heightened potential for losses. Prices for more than a dozen leveraged ETFs tracking Samsung and SK Hynix have nearly halved since their listings in late May, according to Bloomberg.
One single-stock leveraged ETF tracking Samsung, which has $US3.4 billion in assets under management, has fallen about 45 per cent since its debut and is down more than 60 per cent from its June peak.
South Korea's decision to this year greenlight single-stock two times leveraged ETFs has led to rapid market distortions. Because the market is heavily weighted toward a few massive tech names, the mechanical daily rebalancing of these leveraged funds has been blamed for accelerating massive sell-offs and feeding feedback loops during market crashes.
Australia's leveraged ETFs, by contrast, focus more on broad portfolio strategies which track whole sectors, or even the entire index.
And this, combined with the much smaller amount of money involved as well as generally lower risk appetite, means the Australian sharemarket is unlikely to be swept up in the same level of volatility, which has largely been blamed on the introduction of single-stock ETFs, for which Korean regulators and even President Lee Jae Myung have expressed regret for.
"At their current size, and given that Australian leveraged ETFs focus on relatively liquid and index style exposures, they are unlikely to be a major source of market volatility," said ETF Shares chief executive Cliff Man. "That risk would be more significant for less liquid instruments, such as single stock exposures, as seen in the Korean market."
But risks still exist, according to VanEck's Asia Pacific manager director Arian Neiron, who warned that investors should take heed of that divergence between the best and worst-performing locally-listed geared ETFs.
"That spread is the story in itself: gearing amplifies losses just as powerfully as gains."
